title: U.S. Open recap Day 6: Taylor Townsend backs up 2025 run after challenging 12 months
content:
Follow The Athletic’s U.S. Open coverage

Welcome to the U.S. Open briefing, where The Athletic will explain the stories behind the stories on each day of the tournament.

On Day 6, a milestone repeated, a good day and a strange night for the Americans and a resurgent player breaking new ground.

Tennis is the only sport where players aren’t just battling their opponent, the elements and their own range of  on a given day — they’re also competing against their past selves.

Because the sport’s rankings system looks backwards 52 weeks, home favorite Taylor Townsend faced high stakes at the 2026 U.S. Open. Twelve months ago, the 30-year-old matched her career-best result at a Grand Slam by reaching the fourth round. Those points she accumulated in New York last year will fall off at the conclusion of this year’s tournament.

That meant her third-round 6-2, 7-6(3), 6-3 win over No. 15 seed Diana Shnaider on Friday afternoon carried extra meaning.

“I’ve been through so much over this year. I was so nervous coming into this tournament; I didn’t want my ranking to drop. I wanted to prove that I was just as good this year as last year,” Townsend said in a tearful on-court interview.

A former top-ranked junior player and a doubles world No. 1, Townsend has felt the scrutiny of living in the public eye since she was a teenager, compounded by the loneliness of playing a sport where few other players look like her.

Her perspective on her career shifted last year when she got a concussion during the Miami Open, an injury that frightened her because of how deceptive it was — she would feel fine one moment, then try to concentrate or do any physical activity and feel terrible.

She returned to tennis with more gratitude, and the feeling that she isn’t playing to disprove her doubters, but to meet her own expectations.

“I’m the kind of person where when I go through something, I kind of analyze it, and I’m, like, ‘OK, why is this happening and what did I learn from it?’ I’m always asking, ‘What did I learn?’” Townsend said in a news conference.

Townsend hadn’t won a main draw singles match at a Grand Slam all year before her first-round win here. But some excellent serving — and a little pressure from her past self — has propelled her to a fourth-round matchup against Aryna Sabalenka.

She said she’s ready for the challenge.

— Ava Wallace

The American roll got started early on Friday, but later than No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula might have liked. Pegula, the 2024 beaten finalist, got to the fourth round with a comeback win over Canada’s Leylah Fernandez, the 2021 beaten finalist, on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

“I was like, it can’t be that much worse,” Pegula said after a 1-6, 6-4, 6-3 win.

“I think I knew my strategy. I think she played a bit differently than I’ve played her in the past. … But you still know what you have to execute, and I just tried to focus on that.”

From there, things went about as well as an American in New York could have hoped. Emma Navarro, who had not made the fourth round at a major since Wimbledon 2025, knocked off this year’s Wimbledon finalist, Karolína Muchová, 6-3, 7-5.

Frances Tiafoe cruised past Valentin Vacherot, the Monégasque No. 22 seed, 6-4, 6-2, 6-4. Taylor Townsend got the better of Diana Shnaider. Alex Michelsen, who had knocked out higher-seeded compatriot Brandon Nakashima in the previous round, defeated the rising Spaniard Daniel Mérida 7-6(5), 6-4, 6-3. Tommy Paul survived a five-set duel with Alexander Bublik, who beat him in one of the matches of the tournament in 2025. This time around, Paul didn’t just win 6-4, 3-6, 7-6(4), 6-1, 6-3 — he kept his nerve when Bublik took the score from 5-0 to 5-3 in the fifth, having had some painfully tight losses this year.

There were some losses a bit like that for the Americans. Ann Li fell to Wimbledon champion Linda Nosková in three sets after a stirring second-set comeback. The Williams sisters came achingly close to defeating Maya Joint and Chan Hao-ching but lost a match-deciding tiebreak from 5-0 up.

All that happened before No. 8 seed Ben Shelton took to court to cap off the night on Arthur Ashe against Denis Shapovalov. After they traded sets in which the player who should have won failed to do so by self-destructing, Shelton took it home 7-6(3), 6-7(5), 6-3, 6-4.

In his news conference, Michelsen tried to name all the American men who were left. He got most of the way, but he forgot about Taylor Fritz, who has been the most dominant player in the draw so far. He kicks off the action on Arthur Ashe Saturday, against Francisco Cerúndolo, the No. 24 seed from Argentina.

“Hopefully we get some guys into the semis or the finals, and then you never know,” Michelsen said, as they bid to end the wait for an American man to win a major that is at 23 years and counting. Michelsen, like Fritz, is yet to drop a set this tournament.

There’s one issue for all these Americans at the bottom of the men’s draw: Carlos Alcaraz. If Paul, Shelton and Tiafoe or Michelsen keep winning, Alcaraz could face three Americans in a row from the round of 16 until the final.

Matt Futterman

Stefanos Tsitsipas is nothing if not enigmatic.

The two-time Grand Slam finalist, who appeared to be an heir apparent to the stars of the sport five years ago, sank to some depths he hadn’t seen in a long time this year. He’s 27-20 this season and has seen his past 18 months heavily disrupted by injuries, most notably one to his back that left him struggling to walk after exiting this tournament early in 2025.

When Tsitsipas arrived in New York for this year’s U.S. Open, he hadn’t made it past the second round of a Grand Slam since the French Open in 2024.

So, of course, he chose this U.S. Open not just to get to the second week for the first time in his career, but to demonstrate that he has acquired — or at least started to groove — skills that seemed beyond his reach at 28, and which might propel him back toward where he once was.

Earlier in the week, he said success in this tournament was as simple as improving on his game, getting a little better than he has been for much of the year. He cares less about results. He has brought on a new coach, Patrick Mouratoglou, after splitting with his father earlier this year.

And after defeating No. 18 seed Jiří Lehečka 2-6, 6-1, 7-6(3), 6-1, he might have gotten closer to one of his U.S. Open dreams: Playing a late-round match at night on Arthur Ashe.

— Matt Futterman

A 147 mph serve from Ben Shelton, as experienced by Denis Shapovalov:

🤳 Why the U.S. Open disputed two influencers’ accounts of why they had their credentials revoked.

⁉️ And … Why Aryna Sabalenka had to ask a chair umpire to manage the smell of marijuana.

💫 How Venus and Serena Williams reunited one of the last singles superstar doubles teams.

🇺🇸 The depth of American women’s tennis is on full display at the U.S. Open.

📆 For tennis greats, retirement can feel like death. In her final season on tour, Sorana Cîrstea is playing the best tennis of her life.

🗣️ Tennis etiquette at the tournament is back in the discourse. None of this is new.

All times in ET

🎾 Women’s singles: Madison Keys (22) vs. Zheng Qinwen (Q)

11 a.m. on ESPN Unlimited

In an alternative tennis timeline, this might be a match deep in the second week: A banner matchup between 31-year-old Madison Keys, the 2025 Australian Open champion and 23-year-old Zheng Qinwen, the 2024 Olympic gold medalist. It still is a banner matchup, and it might mean even more than a deep run for Zheng, who is finding herself on court again after a lengthy, halting recovery from an elbow injury.

🎾 Women’s singles: Mirra Andreeva (5) vs. Nikola Bartůňková

~ 1 p.m. on ESPN Unlimited

Not so long ago, French Open champion Mirra Andreeva, 19, was the only teenager in the WTA top 100, in a reversal of the tour’s history of prodigies. Bartůňková, who is now 20, became one of a growing number in 2025. This match has the potential to be symphonic, with Bartůňková’s swashbuckling attack meeting Andreeva’s counterpunching durability.

🎾 Women’s singles: Iva Jović (14) vs. Alex Eala (17)

7 p.m. on ESPN2, ESPN Unlimited

Two more rising young stars. Jović, 19, the home hope; Eala, 21, the new sporting hero for the Philippines. Evenly matched in terms of power but with different ways of using it — Eala lacing the ball flat, Jović winning points by a thousand cuts — the key may be who handles the Arthur Ashe Stadium experience better. Oh, and did you know they are best friends?

🎾 Men’s singles: Jakub Menšík (17) vs. Learner Tien (14)

~ 9 p.m. on ESPN Unlimited

Another stylistic clash between young talents to close things out. Menšík, 21, has one of the most devastating serves in the game, but he backs it up with surprising movement for his height and a rock-solid backhand more than the usual forehand crusher. Tien, 20, mostly massages the ball around the court until his opponents are scrambling for their lives, but he can also crack a forehand when he needs to do so.

Tell us what you noticed on the sixth day…
